title: The ancestors
hookLine: God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; many communities add Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah
carry: god of our fathers and mothers

lines: LEAD WITH A NAME THEY TRUST.
cards: How do you introduce yourself to someone important? Often, not with your own name. You lead with a connection.
My grandmother used to talk about you. Your father helped mine when we first arrived. A name someone already trusts opens the door before yours does.
The Amidah opens the same way. After the three steps, after open my lips, the first blessing doesn't say who the person praying is. It says whose family they come from.

teach.b: The first blessing is called Avot: fathers, ancestors.

teach.h: GOD OF ABRAHAM, GOD OF ISAAC...
teach.b: It begins: blessed are You, our God and God of our fathers, God of Abraham, God of Isaac, and God of Jacob. That's straight from the burning bush.

When Moses asks for God's name, God says, in the old Jewish translation, "The LORD, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob." It doesn't say the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.
A Hasidic teaching, which tradition credits to the Baal Shem Tov, hears in that repetition that each one had to find God for himself; Isaac couldn't simply inherit Abraham's faith.
The blessing goes on: the great, the mighty, the awesome God, words from Deuteronomy. Who remembers the kindness of the ancestors, and brings a redeemer to their children's children.
It ends: blessed are You, shield of Abraham. People bow at its start and at its end.

teach.h: SOME ADD SARAH, REBEKAH, RACHEL, LEAH.
teach.b: In recent decades, Reform, Conservative and Reconstructionist prayer books have offered the four mothers: Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah, so the line becomes God of our fathers and our mothers, and in some the ending names Sarah too.

teach.h: GOD OF OUR FATHERS AND MOTHERS.
teach.b: Orthodox communities keep the traditional words. Either way, no one walks up to this prayer alone. You come carrying the people who brought you, and you ask to be heard partly because of them.

how: Avot is the first blessing of every Amidah; people bend the knees and bow at its opening and closing words, and some non-Orthodox prayer books include the matriarchs Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah alongside the patriarchs.

games.q: you're writing a prayer that will be said before God three times a day. how does Avot open?
o: with the name of the person praying.
with the family: God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob.
games.why: it leads with the ancestors, the words God used at the burning bush, before asking for anything.

practice: Say the names of the people who raised you, or who were family to you, in your head or under your breath, then go back a step to their parents, and one more if you can. Where the names run out, notice that too: someone was there.
With each name, think of one thing they handed down, a recipe, a stubbornness, a way of laughing.

wordCard.voice: Avot. Fathers, ancestors. The Amidah's first blessing, which comes before God by naming a family: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and in some communities Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah.

orig.note: Hebrew: fathers, ancestors. the name of the Amidah's first blessing.

carryVoice: Your line: god of our fathers and mothers. Each one, a teaching says, found God anew. Until tomorrow.
